content.p: On 2 June 1941, German paratroopers gathered the people of Kondomari, a village about 18 kilometres west of the port city of Chania on Crete, into the village square. Several men were then picked out, led into the olive groves around the village and shot. Greek City Times describes the killings as an execution carried out by an improvised firing squad, and as the first of a series of reprisals on the island. The killings took place two days after the Allied forces on Crete surrendered, at the end of the Battle of Crete.
content.h2: The island's fight and the German response
content.p: The Battle of Crete began on 20 May 1941 with a German airborne invasion. The Pappas Post writes that the Nazis were dumbfounded by the resistance, having never experienced such ferocious fighting from civilians anywhere else in Europe. Martin Cherrett, on ww2today, says that the civilian population of Crete had joined in the defence of the island alongside Greek and British armed forces.

Some of the early civilian resistance took place near Kandanos in western Crete. According to New Greek TV, local people with the help of a few Selino gendarmes confronted a German force at Floria on 23 May, and on 24 and 25 May they fought advancing troops at the Kandanos gorge. They were outnumbered and withdrew into the mountains.

Even before the battle ended, exaggerated stories circulated that paratroopers had been mutilated or tortured by Cretans. New Greek TV says that later investigations found only a few cases of mutilation, most of them carried out after death. Martin Cherrett, writing on ww2today, says the bodies had been left on the landing grounds in the heat and decomposed quickly. He also says that Hermann Göring, who led the Luftwaffe and the airborne troops, ordered reprisal measures.

War History Online reports that on Crete the German high command ordered that ten civilians be executed for every German soldier killed or wounded. The same piece describes how the occupation of Greece as a whole led to famine, requisitions and mass reprisals, and it puts the wider German killings of Greek civilians at 21,000, a figure that the article attributes to an estimate rather than a count.

Four lorries carrying German paratroopers from the III Battalion of Luftlande-Sturm-Regiment 1 reached Kondomari on 2 June. Greek City Times names the officer in command as Oberleutnant Horst Trebes, and describes him as a former member of the Hitler Youth and the most senior officer of the battalion to come through the battle unwounded. Cherrett quotes a statement by Weixler that gives the unit as a detachment of about twenty-five parachutists of the second battalion, with Trebes, another lieutenant, an interpreter and two sergeants. The two accounts differ on the battalion, and both are shown here.

Cherrett quotes a statement that Franz-Peter Weixler, a German army war correspondent attached to the division, made to the Allies for the later trial of Göring. In that statement Weixler says that the detachment stopped near the village of Malemes, where Trebes showed the men the corpses of several soldiers, already in the process of decay, and incited them against the civilian population. The statement then says the drive continued to Kondomari. Cherrett presents it as Weixler's own account, made after the war.

According to Greek City Times, the villagers were gathered in the square, the women and children were then released, and the hostages were led to the olive groves and shot. The Pappas Post describes the village as having lost most of its male population. Neither page gives a total for those killed, so no figure is given here.

Weixler was a war propaganda photographer, and he photographed the day. Cherrett calls it a rare instance in which there is fairly comprehensive photographic and written evidence of the circumstances of a German shooting of civilians. The Pappas Post says the negatives were found decades later in German federal archives.

Greek City Times credits the discovery to the Greek journalist Vassos Mathiopoulos, who found the negatives in the federal German archives in 1980 without knowing where the shootings had happened. Greek City Times says that journalist Kostas Papapetrou later established the link between the negatives and Kondomari. Greek City Times presents this as the point at which the pictures became widely known.
content.h2: Weixler's own trouble with the regime
content.p: Weixler's story does not end with the photographs. According to Greek City Times, the army let Weixler go after the summer of 1941 on political grounds. He was later accused of high treason, the charge being that he had leaked uncensored material about the paratroopers' activities on Crete, including photographs taken in Kondomari, and that he had helped some Cretans flee. The Gestapo arrested him, he was court-martialled, and he was imprisoned from early 1944.

New Greek TV dates Student's order for a wave of reprisals to the days just after the island's surrender on 31 May. As New Greek TV describes it, the units that had been fought by the islanders were the ones given the task, and the killings were to be done without the usual procedure. Greek City Times and The Pappas Post place the Kondomari killings first in that series, and New Greek TV says German troops reached the village of Kandanos on 3 June 1941.

New Greek TV gives a figure of about 180 residents killed at Kandanos on 3 June. It adds that the Germans slaughtered the livestock, set fire to the houses and razed them, and that Floria and Kakopetro suffered similar treatment. Afterwards the ruined village was declared a dead zone, its survivors were barred from rebuilding it, and German and Greek inscriptions were put up at each entrance. One, as New Greek TV quotes it, said the village had been destroyed in retribution for the murder of 25 German soldiers and would never be rebuilt. War History Online reports that Kandanos has since been rebuilt, and that reproductions of the German signposts are displayed on a local war memorial.

After Germany's surrender, British forces captured Student. The tribunal that sat in May 1947 heard charges that his forces had mistreated and killed prisoners of war on Crete. Greece asked for his extradition, and the request was refused. Greek City Times and War History Online both report that he was found guilty of three of eight charges and sentenced to five years in prison. He was given a medical discharge and freed in 1948. Both pages state that he was never tried for crimes against civilians. He lived until 1978.

Greek City Times reports that Kondomari was later declared a martyred village by Presidential Decree 29. The village's memorial carries the names of those who died. In 2016, the President of the Hellenic Republic laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Heroes in Kandanos after the service, as New Greek TV reports.
